analysis.one_liner: Increases penalties on insurers and providers that violate surprise medical billing rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the Senate health committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2022 No Surprises Act generally bars providers from billing patients for the difference when they get out-of-network care at an in-network hospital or in an emergency, but enforcement has been limited. This bill raises civil penalties for violations to $10,000 per violation, requires payment within 30 days after a dispute ruling, imposes a penalty of three times the disputed amount plus interest for late or missing payments, and requires regular reports to Congress on audits and enforcement. It was introduced in the Senate in July 2025 and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has not acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with employer-sponsored or individual health coverage who could otherwise face surprise bills when a provider or facility violates the No Surprises Act. Stronger penalties give insurers and employers a financial reason to comply, and the 30-day payment rule after dispute rulings means both insurers and providers settle up promptly instead of dragging out payment. Six-month public reporting to Congress makes enforcement visible.

how_it_helps.text: Raises civil penalties to $10,000 per violation, per person affected, when a group health plan or insurer fails to follow the balance billing protections.

Requires a party that loses a payment dispute and owes money to pay within 30 days; if it pays late or not at all, it owes triple the disputed amount plus interest, in addition to the original payment.
Requires the agencies to report to Congress every six months on audits, complaints from patients and providers, enforcement actions, penalties issued, and the most common violations.

analysis.who_pays: Group health plans, health insurers, and out-of-network providers that violate the rules would bear the new $10,000-per-violation penalties and triple-payment late penalties; those costs could partly flow to employers and premiums.

drawbacks.text: The 3x late-payment penalty applies to both sides: plans that pay late, but also nonparticipating providers who fail to return money owed to plans within 30 days of a dispute ruling, which could put financially fragile providers at risk.
Higher penalties and added notification and audit-reporting duties for insurers and employers could add compliance costs that show up in premiums or benefit design.
The bill builds on the existing No Surprises Act framework rather than addressing its broader problems, such as disputes over what the 'out-of-network rate' should be.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain for patients is faster, more reliable resolution of No Surprises Act disputes, and better public information about whether the ban is enforced; the costs are heavier compliance paperwork and financial exposure for plans and providers, some of which could be passed to premiums, and a doubled-edged 3x penalty that also targets providers who drag out disputes. The design is targeted and enforcement-focused rather than a broad overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never took it up, so it died in committee with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 23, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No committee action, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill sat in committee with no further steps in the record.
It attracted one cosponsor, Senator Michael Bennet, a Democrat, giving it sponsorship from both parties but little visible support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and employer plans that violate surprise-billing rules are better off, because the stronger penalties that would apply to them never took effect; patients who get surprise bills gained nothing.

for.name: Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule a markup or advance the bill after its referral, leaving it unacted on.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, but the record contains no votes or other partisan signals to show how the chambers would have split.

industries.industry: Group health plans and health insurers
industries.note: They face up to $10,000-per-person penalties for violating billing protections, 30-day payment deadlines after dispute rulings, and triple-damages late penalties plus audit reporting. Enforcement pressure on them is what protects patients from surprise bills.

industries.industry: Out-of-network providers, facilities, and air ambulance operators
industries.note: The bill gives them stronger tools to collect what they are owed and new weapons against insurers that stall, but it also subjects them to 3x penalties and 30-day deadlines when they owe money back after losing a dispute.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate HELP Committee with a single cosponsor and no committee action; the most likely path is that it dies at the end of the 119th Congress unless it is attached to a larger health package or revived in a future Congress.
